tours.title: Guided zoom-out: from the Sun to the CMB
tours.summary: Five stops that climb from the Solar System to the last-scattering surface.

stops.title: The Sun
stops.caption: The Solar System sits at the coordinate origin of this atlas; the Sun marker is not to scale. The disk around us is the illustrative Milky Way reference, drawn with adopted dimensions rather than measured star positions.
stops.cue: Find the Sun marker inside our illustrated home galaxy.

stops.title: The Milky Way
stops.caption: We look at the Galactic core from 60 kpc away; the Sun orbits about 8.1 kpc from it, so the core's light seen now left about 26,000 years ago. The disk size and bar are adopted literature values, while the arms, dust and colors are illustrative.
stops.cue: Trace the dark dust lanes around the bright Galactic core.

stops.title: The Local Group
stops.caption: Six nearby galaxies with independently measured distances surround us here; Andromeda is about 785 kpc away, so its light left about 2.6 million years ago. DESI positions come from redshift alone, and those inferred within 1 Mpc are hidden by default as a display safeguard, not as corrected distances.
stops.cue: Look for our nearby galaxy companions, each at its own measured distance.

stops.title: The DESI survey
stops.caption: {catalogCount} accepted DESI DR1 observations in this dataset, placed at comoving distances inferred from redshift; the farthest is about 4,831 Mpc away, where the light left about 10 billion years ago. The sky coverage is uneven because the survey observed selected regions, so the dark gaps were not surveyed here and are not confirmed empty.
stops.cue: Each point is a galaxy observation; the gaps also reflect where we have data.

stops.title: The cosmic microwave background
stops.caption: The faint shell marks the approximate last-scattering surface at z ≈ 1090: about 13,884 Mpc away in today's comoving distance (45.3 billion ly), though its light travelled for 13.8 billion years. It is an inferred, illustrative shell, not a physical edge of the universe, and no measured temperature map is shown.
stops.cue: Find the tiny galaxy survey inside this enormous shell of early light.

tours.title: Cosmic road trip
tours.summary: From the Galactic core past the Magellanic Clouds and Andromeda to two named DESI galaxies, the Coma cluster and the whole survey.

stops.title: The Milky Way
stops.caption: Our trip starts 60 kpc from the Galactic core, whose light reaches us after about 26,000 years; the Sun is about 8.1 kpc from it. The disk dimensions are adopted from the literature, and the arms, dust and colors are illustrative.
stops.cue: Trace the dark dust lanes around the bright Galactic core.

stops.title: Large Magellanic Cloud
stops.caption: The Large Magellanic Cloud is about 49.6 kpc away by eclipsing-binary measurement, so its light left about 160,000 years ago. Its round shape and 1.5 kpc size are assumed, its orientation is not measured, and the image-inspired stellar bar, pink emission patches and dust are illustrative, not a measured gas map.
stops.cue: Look for the broad stellar bar and pink patches in this cloud illustration.

stops.title: Small Magellanic Cloud
stops.caption: The Small Magellanic Cloud is about 62.4 kpc away, also from eclipsing binaries, so its light left about 200,000 years ago. Its projected ellipse and angle are measured, but its half-light size is assumed from a catalog diameter and its image-inspired diffuse stellar body, wing, dust and depth are illustrative, not a measured gas map.
stops.cue: Notice the softer, uneven glow of this smaller cloud illustration.

stops.title: Andromeda
stops.caption: Andromeda (M31) lies about 785 kpc away by the tip of the red giant branch, so we see it as it was about 2.6 million years ago. Its disk size, axis ratio and sky angle are measured; the single-disk light and dust arcs are guided by telescope images, with illustrative depth, feature placement and colors.
stops.cue: Follow the dark dust arcs around the bright center of this illustrated disk.

stops.title: M32 and M110
stops.caption: M32 (about 805 kpc, uncertain by roughly 80 kpc, from RR Lyrae stars) and M110 (about 824 kpc, tip of the red giant branch) have separately measured distances and are not forced onto Andromeda's distance shell. Their measured half-light ellipses are drawn with illustrative smooth light profiles; M110's light left about 2.7 million years ago.
stops.cue: Look beside Andromeda for its small, smooth companions.

stops.title: Triangulum
stops.caption: Triangulum (M33) is about 809 kpc away by the tip of the red giant branch; its light left about 2.6 million years ago. The disk scale, projected ellipse and angle are measured, while its single-disk model, patchy arms and pink emission regions are guided by telescope images, with illustrative depth, feature placement and colors.
stops.cue: Look for loose, patchy arms and pink accents in this illustrated disk.

stops.title: NGC 3982
stops.caption: NGC 3982 is a DESI DR1 galaxy whose position comes from its measured redshift: about 16.6 Mpc, so its light left about 54 million years ago. Its individually fitted shape is one of the two original close-up previews; its winding arms and dust follow telescope-image references, with illustrative feature placement, depth and colors.
stops.cue: Follow the closely winding arms in this image-inspired galaxy model.

stops.title: NGC 4026
stops.caption: NGC 4026 is the second original close-up preview, placed at about 14.6 Mpc from its measured redshift; the light left about 47 million years ago. Its smooth lenticular light follows the fitted profile and telescope-image appearance; redshift distances carry peculiar-velocity and fitting error, so this position is inferred rather than directly measured.
stops.cue: Notice the narrow, smooth spindle and its brighter center.

stops.title: Coma cluster
stops.caption: Look for the central gathering of galaxy points: the Coma cluster (Abell 1656), centered on its NED position and redshift z = 0.024, about 106 Mpc away, where light left about 340 million years ago. Each survey point is a galaxy observation; internal motions stretch redshift distances along our line of sight, and a sky-and-redshift window indicates possible association rather than true membership.
stops.cue: Look for the central gathering of points; each is a galaxy observation.

stops.title: The DESI survey
stops.caption: The road ends at the survey: {catalogCount} accepted DESI DR1 observations in this dataset, placed at comoving distances inferred from redshift, reaching about 4,831 Mpc where light left about 10 billion years ago. Coverage follows where DESI pointed, so dark regions were not surveyed here and are not confirmed empty.
stops.cue: Zoom out to the whole survey and trace its branching pattern of galaxy points.
